summary.central_question: How will the simultaneous shocks of 2020 affect different emerging economies, and what policy responses do they require?
summary.main_thesis: The shocks create many different emerging market crises: strong countries should self-insure, while the official sector (IMF, World Bank, central banks) must replace retreating private capital for the weaker ones.

content.text: How will the simultaneous shocks of 2020 affect different emerging economies, and what policy responses do they require?
content.reason: A common shock can demand different responses depending on each country's starting position.

passages.source_excerpt: But the impact of these shocks will differ radically, as will the needed global policy response.

content.text: Four simultaneous shocks hit emerging economies: an oil and commodity price collapse below breakevens, a manufacturing trade shock from shutdowns, a sudden stop in private flows, and reduced cross-border dollar financing.
content.reason: Commodity prices below balance of payments breakevens create external financing gaps for exporters.

passages.source_excerpt: An oil price shock that has sent the price of Brent oil down to under $25

content.text: The shocks offset each other in some cases, as with Turkey, which gains from cheap oil but loses exports, tourism and access to loan rollovers.
content.reason: A country's net exposure depends on the sum of its gains and losses across several channels.

passages.source_excerpt: These shocks can have offsetting impacts. A country that imports oil, for example, Turkey, will benefit from lower energy prices.

content.text: In a crisis, finance shifts back to banks with central bank access, which squeezes their balance sheets and limits dollar credit even to creditworthy borrowers.
content.reason: In stress, funding migrates to institutions with lender-of-last-resort access, straining their capacity.

passages.source_excerpt: Global finance is now quickly being re-intermediated through banks, as they offer a form of stability that the “shadow” (non-bank) financial system cannot replicate in a crisis.

content.text: Countries divide into those with strong external balance sheets, which can self-insure, and those with weaker ones, which face the pressing problems.
content.reason: Net external asset positions decide whether a country can absorb a shock or must adjust or borrow.

passages.source_excerpt: Some countries have relatively strong balance sheets and are thus fairly well equipped to handle these shocks on their own.

content.text: Saudi Arabia and Russia hold about $500 billion in reserves each, and the smaller GCC states hold over $1 trillion in sovereign wealth funds, so strong oil exporters can self-finance the revenue shortfall.
content.reason: Accumulated reserves let a country delay adjustment to a terms of trade shock.

passages.source_excerpt: The Saudis have around $500 billion in reserves, and the Russians a comparable sum and the added advantage of a floating currency.

content.text: Oil exporters with large reserves and sovereign wealth funds should draw them down rather than adjust immediately.
content.reason: Reserves are built precisely to be spent in a shock.

passages.source_excerpt: Those buffers can and should be used.

content.text: Asian surplus countries lose value on their offshore portfolios, but this only becomes a problem where the assets sit on leveraged, thinly capitalized balance sheets, such as some life insurers.
content.reason: Asset losses threaten stability mainly when the holders are leveraged.

passages.source_excerpt: That’s only an immediate problem if the assets are held on levered balance sheets—some insurers, for example, are pretty thinly capitalized

content.text: Taiwan's foreign assets far exceed its foreign liabilities, so despite its insurers' large hedging needs the country faces no external financial risk.
content.reason: A net external creditor faces credit risk on what it lent, not funding risk.

passages.source_excerpt: But it has significantly more foreign assets than foreign debt. It faces the same risk as other creditors, namely that it lent out funds that it may not get back in full or on time.

content.text: Losses at the financial institutions of strong-balance-sheet countries can be absorbed domestically, on the assumption that the government is able and willing to recapitalize them.
content.reason: A solvent sovereign with fiscal space can backstop its own financial sector.

passages.source_excerpt: But any shortfall in the life insurers equity can be made up domestically, through a government recapitalization.

content.text: Home central banks should supply dollar hedges to their institutions, regulators should be flexible, and Fed swap lines and the repo facility could be repurposed to help.
content.reason: A public balance sheet should backstop private leveraged institutions when hedging markets seize up.

passages.source_excerpt: Their “home” central banks in my view need to—and can—step up, and their regulators need to show flexibility.

content.text: Countries with strong external balance sheets can weather the shock by using their public balance sheets.
content.reason: Self-insurance works when the public sector holds enough net external assets.

passages.source_excerpt: Countries with strong external balance sheets consequently can weather the storm if they act decisively

content.text: Countries with more external debt than liquid reserves face the hardest problems, because private financing disappears exactly when they need it.
content.reason: Private capital is procyclical and withdraws from the weakest borrowers first.

passages.source_excerpt: In a crisis, those countries that most need financing are the least able to get it.

content.text: Funding needs come in two kinds, short-term dollar trade finance and medium- to long-term balance of payments gaps from terms of trade shocks, inflow stops or bank runs, and each needs a different tool.
content.reason: Liquidity needs and solvency-like external gaps call for different instruments.

passages.source_excerpt: I would differentiate here between two different kinds of funding needs:

content.text: Balance of payments shortfalls are properly met from national reserves, with the IMF and World Bank as the backstop when reserves run short.
content.reason: External financing gaps are first covered by own reserves and then by multilateral lenders.

passages.source_excerpt: Those are the kinds of financing shortfalls normally met out of national reserves—with the IMF and the World Bank stepping in to provide additional financing when national reserves are insufficient.

content.text: Essential imports such as food and medicine should take priority over on-time repayment of external bonds.
content.reason: Debt service should not crowd out a country's basic humanitarian needs in an emergency.

passages.source_excerpt: no country should have to face a situation where it is unable to pay for food and medical supplies simply because it has an external bond coming due

content.text: Fed swap lines are suited to dollar funding of intermediaries, not to covering balance of payments shortfalls, as the 2008 experience shows.
content.reason: A liquidity facility for intermediaries cannot substitute for external financing of a country.

passages.source_excerpt: The Fed’s swap lines historically have not been used to make up for financing shortfalls from a classic fall off in portfolio inflows

content.text: The author's 2005 forecast with Roubini, that central banks would stop financing the U.S. deficit first, was wrong: private credit intermediation broke down first.
content.reason: External deficits need both official buyers to bear currency risk and private intermediaries to bear credit risk.

passages.source_excerpt: The system of private credit risk intermediation broke down well before the world’s central banks lost their appetite for FX intervention (contrary to a forecast that I made with Dr. Roubini back in 2005).

content.text: Brender and Pisani, along with the author's Iceland conference paper, explain how the U.S. deficit before 2008 depended on both official reserve accumulation and private credit intermediation.
content.reason: Past crises show how funding structures break down.

passages.source_excerpt: as Brender and Pisani laid out so clearly, in a still under appreciated monograph

content.text: Central banks, with Fed help and national export-import banks, can address trade finance, building on BIS proposals.
content.reason: Short-term dollar trade finance gaps are a liquidity problem that central banks can fill.

passages.source_excerpt: Agustin Carstens of the BIS has provided some exceptionally helpful suggestions

content.text: The IMF should make an SDR allocation to raise global reserves, with reserve-rich countries lending their SDRs back.
content.reason: When the global demand for reserves jumps, the official sector should create more.

passages.source_excerpt: Now is the time when the IMF can and should use its ability to create global reserves through what’s called an “SDR allocation”

content.text: An SDR allocation alone is insufficient because it is distributed by quota rather than need, so the IMF and the multilateral development banks also need more lending capacity.
content.reason: A tool distributed by formula rather than need will miss the countries in greatest need.

passages.source_excerpt: But SDRs are distributed according to a country’s IMF quota, not according to the amount of reserves a country now needs

content.text: Bilateral creditors should defer payments and private bondholders should voluntarily extend 2020 maturities.
content.reason: A voluntary maturity extension beats default for both creditor and debtor.

passages.source_excerpt: private creditors should also be encouraged to extend the maturity of bonds that are coming due in 2020

reasons: links: `REC5` supports `K` joins L5→L5, which no hand-drawn supports link does

content.text: Private creditors prefer full repayment and may resist maturity extensions.
content.reason: Individual creditors gain from being paid even when collective restraint serves everyone better.

passages.source_excerpt: Of course, private creditors would rather be paid.

content.text: The shocks create many different emerging market crises: strong countries should self-insure, while the official sector (IMF, World Bank, central banks) must replace retreating private capital for the weaker ones.
content.reason: Official finance should substitute for procyclical private finance in a crisis.

passages.source_excerpt: When private capital retreats, the official sector needs to advance—and with creativity, sufficient resources can be mobilized to limit the global shock.

content.text: These measures will not prevent a massive downturn; they only aim to preserve the financial infrastructure for the recovery.
content.reason: Emergency liquidity limits damage but cannot offset a real shock.

passages.source_excerpt: While none of this will prevent a massive global downturn, it is crisis economics

content.text: Broader reforms are explicitly put off until after the recovery.
content.reason: Structural reform is best sequenced after crisis containment.

passages.source_excerpt: And when that bounce back happens, many more reforms will be needed.
